newsitem.title: UK: Euro crude outlook - Nigeria may counter sloppy N.Sea.
newsitem.headline: Euro crude outlook - Nigeria may counter sloppy N.Sea.

text.p: Improved refining margins and the prospect of nearly three million barrels of North Sea Brent leaving the region this week will not prevent an overhang of prompt barrels pushing the benchmark Brent market lower, traders said.

While differentials for other North Sea and Mediterranean sour grades are expected to follow suit, civil disturbances and crude production cuts in Nigeria should support prices in the West African market, traders said.
"I see one ULCC leaving the (North Sea) -- We definitely need that but it's not enough," said one senior trader for a European major.

A trading house had chartered the ULCC to head to the U.S. Gulf Coast, shipping sources said, but a May Brent/WTI spread of just $1.30 a barrel on Thursday was seen as too narrow to spark an exodus of North Sea barrels across the Atlantic.
Traders said on top of plentiful early April Brents, other North Sea grades were also in abundance.
Forties, which typically commands a premium to Dated Brent, slid to a discount last week, along with Norwegian grades Oseberg and Ekofisk.
A rise in refining margins at a complex Rotterdam plant of 57 cents last week to $2.00 a barrel has had little impact on demand.

"Refining margins are better but there's simply no more demand," a North Sea trader said. "We have to see a steeper contango for people to start putting significant amounts into storage...and even then the oversupply would just be pushed later into the month."

Traders expected pressure at the front end of the market to pull the market's contango wider. Wet Brent traded at an 80-cent discount to May forward prices while intermonth spreads showed prices rising steadily through to the summer.

Sour crudes in Mediterranean are also expected to slide further, after regional benchmark Urals shed some ten cents last week. The extent of further falls will depend on the size of the April loading programme at Novorossiisk, traders said.
"It's a weak market. Deals keep being done below the last one done," a local refiner said.
Bucking the trend could be the West African market, where continued Nigerian civil unrest could disrupt crude exports and send prices rising.
